title: Cornish Fairings
subtitle: crisp ginger biscuits from Cornwall
excerpt: Cornish fairings are thin, crisp ginger biscuits that crackle on the surface as they bake. Golden syrup gives them their characteristic chewy centre while the edges go properly crunchy. Makes about 24 biscuits.
sourceNotes: Fairings were biscuits and small sweets sold at fairs and markets across Britain. In Cornwall, the ginger biscuit version became particularly well established, and Cornish fairings are now protected under a Traditional Speciality Guaranteed status in the UK. The biscuits are associated with the firm of Furniss in Truro, which has been making them commercially since the 1880s, though domestic versions appear in Cornish recipe collections throughout the 19th century. The characteristic crackled surface comes from the combination of golden syrup and bicarbonate of soda, which causes the biscuit to spread and crack as it bakes.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked biscuits in a tin with parchment between layers. Thaw at room temperature.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Store in an airtight tin for up to a week. They crisp further on the second day.

glossaryTerms.definition: Small biscuits or sweets traditionally sold at fairs in Britain. Cornish fairings specifically refers to the ginger biscuits made in Cornwall, now with protected Traditional Speciality Guaranteed status in the UK.

content.text: spread out thin in the oven and crack across the surface as the bicarbonate of soda reacts with the golden syrup and heat. The result is a biscuit that is crisp at the edges and slightly soft at the centre when it comes out of the oven, then firms all the way through as it cools. The ginger flavour is prominent; mixed spice adds a background warmth.

The dough is made by rubbing butter into spiced flour, then stirring in golden syrup to bring it together. It should be slightly sticky but workable. Roll small balls and place them well apart on lined trays: these biscuits spread considerably. Do not flatten before baking; they spread themselves in the oven.
Heat the oven to 175°C fan (195°C conventional). Line two large baking trays with baking parchment.

Put {{plain-flour}} of flour, {{ginger-ground}} of ginger, {{mixed-spice}} of mixed spice, {{bicarbonate-of-soda}} of bicarbonate of soda, {{baking-powder}} of baking powder, and {{salt-table}} of salt into a bowl. Rub in {{unsalted-butter}} of cold butter until it looks like breadcrumbs. Stir in {{caster-sugar}} of sugar.
Warm {{golden-syrup}} of golden syrup slightly if it is stiff (a few seconds in a microwave works). Stir into the dry ingredients until the dough comes together. It will be slightly sticky.
Roll teaspoon-sized portions of dough into balls. Place on the lined trays with at least 5 cm between each: they spread considerably. Do not flatten.

Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until the biscuits have spread, cracked across the surface, and are a deep amber colour. Leave on the tray for 5 minutes before transferring to a wire rack: they are very fragile when hot.

items.symptom: Biscuits do not spread and crack
items.cause: Not enough golden syrup, or dough too firm
items.fix: Warm the syrup slightly before adding. The dough should be sticky, not stiff.

items.symptom: Biscuits burn on the base before the top cooks
items.cause: Dark baking tray, or tray placed too low in the oven
items.fix: Use a light-coloured or heavy baking tray. Place in the middle of the oven and check from 8 minutes.

items.symptom: Biscuits stay soft rather than crisping
items.cause: Stored in an airtight tin while still warm, trapping steam
items.fix: Cool completely on a wire rack before storing. They crisp as they cool.

content.text: Cornish fairings were sold at the fairs that moved through the market towns of Cornwall from the 16th century onwards. The fairs were held for trade in livestock, cloth, and goods, and sellers of biscuits and sweets set up stalls on the margins. The ginger biscuit that became the Cornish fairing was probably established by the late 18th century and commercialised in the 19th. They are sold in bakeries and shops throughout Cornwall, often in paper bags, and eaten as a snack. The protected status TSG confirms that the Cornish fairing is a genuine regional product with a specific recipe and history, not just a generic ginger biscuit.
